OIIX.name: FIR Tehran
OIIX.conflictType: Interstate conflict — Iran vs Israel/US (fragile ceasefire)
OIIX.narrative: EASA's CZIB-2026-04 reflects a ceasefire that has held since April 2026 but remains fragile, with an elevated Iranian air-defence posture that raises the risk of civil aircraft being misidentified. EASA has warned escalation could resume with little notice. The eastern part of the FIR was partially reopened for overflights in June 2026 while the western part remained closed, but EASA's current CZIB continues to advise against operations at any altitude. The primary risk is misidentification of civil aircraft by air-defence systems during periods of heightened tension — a risk demonstrated by the shoot-down of Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran in Jan 2020. Most Europe-Asia traffic continues to route south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan.

cross.detail: July 2026: The ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Very few international operators are using Iranian airspace. Several states continue to warn against operations in the OIIX/Tehran FIR, consistent with EASA's current CZIB. Key events: March 2026: FIR closed following large-scale US and Israeli strikes on Iranian military targets and Iranian missile/drone retaliation. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes. Oct 2024: Israel and Iran carried out missile attacks against each other. Jan 2020: Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 shot down over Tehran after misidentification.

ORBB.name: FIR Baghdad
ORBB.conflictType: Non-state armed groups (IBMGs) + Iranian missile/drone spillover
ORBB.narrative: Despite the regional ceasefire, EASA cites recurrent Iranian drone and ballistic-missile strikes reaching Iraqi airspace, alongside the continued presence of Iranian-backed militant groups (IBMGs), as reasons the Baghdad FIR remains a do-not-operate zone. The primary risks are missile and drone activity linked to regional conflicts, misidentification by air-defence systems operated by local and foreign military forces, and an ongoing threat from terrorist groups possessing portable anti-aircraft weaponry. The FIR was reopened to overflights following the US-Iran ceasefire in June 2026, with north-south routes available, though most Europe-Asia traffic still routes south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan.

cross.detail: July 2026: The ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Iraqi airspace remains open to overflights and some operators continue using it, but EASA's current CZIB advises against operations at any altitude. Key events: March 2026: FIR closed following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent Iranian retaliation. June 2025: Airspace closed following Israeli missile attack on Iran; missiles and drones transited Iraqi airspace. Apr 2024: Airspace closed due to Iranian drone and missile strike on Israel. Apr 2023: Drone and missile attacks in northern Iraq launched from Turkey and Iran, including strikes near ORSU and ORER. Oct 2021: US operators permitted to overfly the ORBB/Baghdad FIR above FL320 under updated FAA restrictions.

OLBB.name: FIR Beirut
OLBB.narrative: A Trilateral Framework Agreement between Israel, Lebanon and the US (26 June 2026) is a step toward consolidating the ceasefire, but EASA notes its long-term implementation is uncertain, and that Lebanon has not shown it can proactively manage airspace risk. Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon have continued despite repeated ceasefire extensions and diplomatic efforts. The primary risks are military activity linked to the Israel-Hezbollah conflict and the wider regional security situation, including missile and drone activity, and GNSS spoofing and jamming reported in the FIR from Nov 2023 onwards. Some states allow limited operations to OLBA/Beirut provided arrivals and departures remain over the Mediterranean Sea.

cross.detail: July 2026: The ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon continue, and most international operators avoid the OLBB/Beirut FIR. Several states maintain long-standing warnings, consistent with EASA's current CZIB advising against operations at any altitude. Key events: Oct 2024: Israel launched a ground operation against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon. Nov 2023 - ongoing: GNSS spoofing and jamming reported in the FIR.

OJAC.name: FIR Amman
OJAC.conflictType: Missile/drone overflight risk (regional spillover, no direct conflict on Jordanian soil)
OJAC.narrative: Jordan's airspace has repeatedly seen Iranian missiles and drones pass through en route to other targets, intercepted by Jordanian and allied air defences. Jordanian authorities have not published any airspace restrictions of their own despite this activity. EASA has issued an Information Note advising operators to take the potential risk into account before operating in the OJAC/Amman FIR. The FIR remained open throughout the Iran conflict, although missile and drone activity affected several neighbouring countries.

cross.detail: July 2026: The ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Jordanian airspace remains open and operating normally. EASA's current Information Note advises operators to take the potential risk into account before operating in the OJAC/Amman FIR. Key events: Apr 2024: Jordan temporarily closed its airspace during the Iranian drone and missile attack on Israel. Oct 2023: Jordan intercepted drones and missiles transiting its airspace during regional escalation.

OKAC.name: FIR Kuwait
OKAC.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OKAC.narrative: Kuwait hosts major US military facilities, making it a plausible target for Iranian retaliation and increasing the risk of civil aircraft being caught up in an attack or an air-defence response. Missile and drone strikes damaged OKKK/Kuwait airport in March 2026. The FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict and is currently open for arrivals and departures only, with overflights remaining prohibited. EASA's current CZIB advises against operations at any altitude.

cross.detail: July 2026: The ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Kuwait has been directly affected; the OKAC/Kuwait FIR is open for arrivals and departures only — overflights remain prohibited. EASA's current CZIB advises against operations at any altitude. Key events: March 2026: Missile and drone strikes damaged OKKK/Kuwait airport. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes across the region.

OBBB.name: FIR Bahrain
OBBB.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OBBB.narrative: As with Kuwait and Qatar, the US military presence in Bahrain is the main driver of EASA's risk assessment for this FIR. The OBBB/Bahrain FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before reopening to normal overflight operations. Iranian missile and drone attacks targeted several Gulf states in March 2026, with incidents affecting airspace around Bahrain. EASA's current CZIB advises against operations at any altitude.

cross.detail: July 2026: The ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Bahraini airspace remains open to overflights. EASA's current CZIB advises against operations at any altitude. Key events: March 2026: Iranian missile and drone attacks targeted several Gulf states, including incidents affecting airspace around Bahrain. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the region.

OTDF.name: FIR Doha
OTDF.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OTDF.narrative: Qatar hosts significant US forces and has itself been targeted by Iranian strikes during the recent escalation, including a missile strike reported at Al Udeid Air Base near Doha in March 2026, keeping it on EASA's do-not-operate list even as operational conditions ease. The OTDF/Doha FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before reopening to normal overflight operations. EASA's current CZIB advises against operations at any altitude.

cross.detail: July 2026: The ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Qatari airspace remains open and operating largely normally. EASA's current CZIB advises against operations at any altitude. Key events: March 2026: Iranian missile strike reported at Al Udeid Air Base near Doha. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the region.

OMAE.name: FIR Emirates
OMAE.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OMAE.narrative: The UAE's proximity to the Strait of Hormuz and its role as a regional hub keep it firmly within EASA's risk assessment, despite being operationally busy.

OOMM.name: FIR Muscat — west of 58°E only
OOMM.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OOMM.narrative: Unlike other Gulf FIRs, only the western portion of Omani/Gulf of Oman waters is covered — reflecting where commercial vessel attacks and Strait of Hormuz tension actually concentrate. Oman itself remained open throughout the Iran conflict and is a key part of the main southern bypass route (Egypt-Saudi-Oman) used by many operators for Europe-Asia traffic. EASA's current CZIB advises against operations over the waters of the Gulf of Oman within the OOMM/Muscat FIR west of 58°E.

cross.detail: July 2026: The ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Omani airspace remains open and carries significant Europe-Asia overflight traffic on the southern bypass route. The primary risk is spillover of missile or drone activity from conflicts elsewhere in the region. Key events: June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the Gulf region. Oct 2024: Israel and Iran carried out missile attacks against each other, leading many operators to avoid airspace between the two countries.

OSTT.name: FIR Damascus
OSTT.narrative: EASA's longest-running Middle East bulletin (19 revisions since 2017) reflects a still-unresolved multi-actor conflict. Traffic patterns have shifted: OSTT quietly reopened to some regional carriers in early 2025 as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq corridor, even though most Western operators continue to avoid it. The primary risks are military activity including Israeli airstrikes targeting Iranian and Hezbollah-linked positions, and the potential for misidentification by air-defence systems. Several countries continue to prohibit or advise against operations in the FIR.

cross.detail: July 2026: The ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Syrian airspace remains high risk, but some regional operators have started using it again as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq routing. Key events: March 2026: FIR closed following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent Iranian retaliation. Dec 2024: Syrian airspace temporarily closed following the fall of the Assad regime. Oct 2023: Airstrikes damaged runways at OSDI/Damascus and OSAP/Aleppo airports. Feb 2020: An A320 approaching Damascus diverted after being caught in crossfire during Israeli airstrikes. Sep 2018: Russian IL-20 shot down in error near the Syria-Cyprus FIR boundary.

OYSC.name: FIR Sana'a only
OYSC.conflictType: Civil war + interstate spillover (Red Sea attacks)
OYSC.narrative: This bulletin covers only the Sana'a FIR, not the whole of Yemen. The ongoing civil war and Houthi involvement in the wider regional conflict keep the risk assessment unchanged since 2017. The primary risk is intentional targeting by terrorist groups with access to sophisticated anti-aircraft weaponry. Civil aircraft are also at risk from high-intensity military operations including explosive drones and missiles. Saudi and Israeli airstrikes can occur at any time, including in the capital Sana'a. OYSN/Sanaa Airport has been closed since Dec 2024 due to damage from Israeli airstrikes. US operators can use offshore routes UT702 and M999; other states permit flights on overwater portions of the FIR.

cross.detail: Yemen remains an active conflict zone; the vast majority of the OYSC/Sanaa FIR should be avoided. Several countries prohibit overflights of any land portion of the FIR. Saudi airspace to the north and Somali airspace to the south also carry risks. Key events: Jul 2026: Yemen's government carried out an airstrike on the runway at OYSN/Sanaa Airport to stop an Iranian aircraft from landing. Dec 2024 - ongoing: OYSN/Sanaa Airport closed due to damage from Israeli airstrikes in Dec 2024 and May 2025. Jan 2024: US and UK carried out airstrikes against Houthi rebels in response to missile and drone attacks in the Red Sea. Sep 2023: Houthi drone attacks near the Yemen-Saudi border. Apr-Oct 2022: All parties agreed a ceasefire. 2018-2022: Frequent Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa and other targets in retaliation for Houthi drone attacks. 2017: OYSN/Sanaa Airport badly damaged by coalition airstrikes.

UUWV.name: FIR Moscow and others (west of 60°E)
UUWV.conflictType: Interstate war — Russian invasion of Ukraine (air-defence risk)
UUWV.narrative: Issued after the likely accidental shoot-down of Azerbaijan Airlines flight 8243 near Grozny in December 2024, this bulletin reflects the risk that Russian air-defence systems responding to Ukrainian strikes pose to civil aircraft, compounded by widespread GNSS interference. Drone attacks across Russia have been escalating, reaching as far as Siberia, and Russian air-defence systems using surface-to-air missiles capable of reaching all altitudes have been active across wide areas including around Moscow. Most operators avoid Russian airspace completely.

cross.detail: The primary risk is unintended targeting of civil aircraft by military systems near the Russia-Ukraine border, including misidentification (as with MAS17, UIA752). Ukraine's airspace has been fully closed to civil aviation since the Russian invasion in Feb 2022. Several countries prohibit operators from using Russian airspace near FIR boundaries with Ukraine. Key events: Jan 2025: EASA issued a new CZIB recommending against flights in western Russia (anywhere west of 60°E) following the shoot-down of a passenger jet at URMG/Grozny on Dec 25, 2024. Jan 2024: Military transport aircraft crashed in Russian airspace near Belgorod, approx 20nm from the Ukrainian border; both Russia and Ukraine accused each other of shooting it down. Aug 2023: Private jet carrying Wagner mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin crashed en route from Moscow to St Petersburg on Aug 23. July 2023 - ongoing: Increasing drone strikes on targets in Moscow and surrounding regions, with some drones damaging buildings and Moscow airports forced to close temporarily on multiple occasions.

UKBV.name: All Ukrainian FIRs
UKBV.narrative: In force since the day of the invasion, this remains one of the clearest and most stable prohibitions in this dataset — Ukraine itself has closed its FIRs to civil traffic by NOTAM. The primary risk is unintended targeting of civil aircraft by military, including misidentification (as with MAS17, UIA752). A secondary risk is potential loss of Ukrainian ATC service at short notice. Russia, Belarus and Moldova have also closed large sections of their own airspace near their FIR boundaries with Ukraine.

cross.detail: Ukraine closed its entire airspace to all civil traffic on Feb 24, 2022, due to a military invasion by Russia. All major countries that regularly issue airspace warnings (the US, UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, and others) have issued total flight bans for Ukraine. Prior to February 2022, there were two areas of concern: the conflict in the far east of the country (affecting UKDV/Dnipro FIR) and the double claim over ATC and airspace in Crimea (UKFV/URFV/Simferopol FIR).

HSSS.name: FIR Khartoum
HSSS.conflictType: Civil war — Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) vs Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
HSSS.narrative: The ongoing SAF–RSF civil war has put anti-aircraft artillery, MANPADS and SAM systems into play across the whole of Sudanese airspace, keeping the entire Khartoum FIR off-limits. HSSK/Khartoum airport is closed but NOTAMs are not being issued. A contingency plan with published overflight routes via HSPN/Port Sudan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and South Sudan is available. The primary risk for any unplanned diversion is security on the ground, including reports of passenger jets being targeted by gunfire at HSSK/Khartoum airport. A secondary risk is Sudan's proximity to South Sudan, which has poor ATC provision for overflights below FL245.

cross.detail: Sudan remains closed to all civilian flights following the military coup in April 2023, with ongoing fighting between government and militant forces. Several countries have issued warnings advising operators not to enter Sudanese airspace due to risks from anti-aircraft weaponry and military activity. In South Sudan, air navigation services remain suspended above FL245. Key events: Nov 2025: Il-76 reportedly shot down by a surface-to-air missile near Babanusa, southern Sudan. May 2025: Drone attack targeting critical infrastructure including HSPN/Port Sudan airport. Oct 2024: Foreign-registered cargo aircraft shot down by local militia over North Darfur, near the border with Chad. Apr 2023: Military coup on Apr 15; Sudan's airspace closed, South Sudan's airspace closed above FL245. Oct 2021: Military coup on Oct 25; HSSK/Khartoum airport closed for two days with all flights suspended.

HLLL.name: FIR Tripoli
HLLL.narrative: Libya's two rival governments and various non-state armed actors create a real risk of misidentification when crossing between areas controlled by different authorities. The one carve-out is for coastal airport approaches made from over the sea. The primary risk is misidentification by Libyan air-defence systems or militia — including threats to shoot down aircraft operating in western Libya and at HLLM/Tripoli Mitiga airport. Military activity has been reported over the high seas operating as OAT or without ATC contact. Reliable ATC services cannot be guaranteed, with regular ATS and radar outages and severe VHF limitations across the FIR.
HLLL.restrictionLabel: Do not operate, except flights to coastal airports approached from the sea, subject to ATC contact and your own risk assessment

cross.detail: A civil war has been ongoing since 2014. The HLLL/Tripoli FIR should be avoided entirely. A total flight ban applies for US operators; several other countries have warnings in place. Risk remains high across Libya at all flight levels. Key events: August 2023: Major evacuation of aircraft from Tripoli due to violent clashes and gunfire at Mitiga airport. July 2023: Italy cancelled its 10-year ban on flights to/from Libya. Aug 2022: Militia air-defence forces claimed to have shot down a US drone operating near Benghazi. June 2022: Failed militia attempt to seize control of government offices resulted in armed clashes and suspension of flights at HLLM/Mitiga airport. Jan 2020: Multiple airstrikes targeted HLLM/Mitiga airport. Nov 2019: Militia advancing on Tripoli declared a no-fly-zone, threatening to shoot down civil aircraft attempting to fly to HLLM/Mitiga airport. 2014: HLLT/Tripoli airport closed after rival militia clashes destroyed most facilities; most flights now operate from HLLM/Mitiga airport.

DRRR.name: Malian territory, especially the north-east
DRRR.conflictType: Insurgency — non-state armed groups active across the Sahel
DRRR.narrative: Non-state armed groups operating in Mali, particularly in the north-east, are assessed to have MANPADS and SAM missile capability, which is why the restriction is altitude-based rather than a total ban. The primary risks include MANPADS and other surface-to-air weapons, indirect fire near airports, and the potential for misidentification or spillover from military activity; low-level and airport-phase operations carry the highest exposure. ATS in Mali is provided by the GOOO/Dakar and DRRR/Niamey FIRs, which have a long-standing restriction for overflights of Mali to published ATS routes at FL320 and above. Several countries advise operations at or above FL250 or FL260 and avoiding GATB/Timbuktu, GAGO/Gao and GAKL/Kidal.

cross.detail: The conflict in northern and central Mali has continued since 2012 and the security situation remains volatile. The US advises caution at all levels due to ongoing fighting, expanding militant activity, and the presence of a state-run paramilitary force operating anti-aircraft systems, military aircraft, UAS and electronic warfare equipment. Key events: April 2026: Security situation escalated sharply. On April 25, multiple armed groups carried out coordinated attacks nationwide against state and military targets, with gunfire and explosions reported near GABS/Bamako. France issued a new airspace warning advising against operations to/from GABS or its use as an alternate. Sep 2024: Insurgents breached GABS/Bamako and set the presidential jet on fire; the airport closed temporarily. Dec 2023: Germany prohibited operators below FL260 in northern Mali; commercial flights to GATB/Timbuktu cancelled after shelling near the airport; a military jet crashed near GAGO/Gao, possibly shot down. Aug 2020: All airports closed for two days during a military coup; Bamako ACC remained operational and overflights were unaffected. Apr 2018: Militants attacked UN bases near GATB/Timbuktu using indirect fire and vehicle bombs. Jan 2017 and Nov 2016: Vehicle bomb and rocket attacks targeted GAGO/Gao and GATB/Timbuktu airports.

HCSM.name: Somali airspace
HCSM.conflictType: Insurgency — Al-Shabaab and related terrorist groups
HCSM.narrative: Terrorist organisations operating in Somalia are assessed to have confirmed anti-aircraft weaponry, possibly including MANPADS, driving the same FL260 altitude floor as Mali. The primary risk is targeting of overflying aircraft at lower flight levels. A secondary risk is from unauthorised ATC units issuing conflicting climb/descent instructions on the same frequency as Mogadishu Control — multiple reports received since Feb 2024. From Nov 2025, Somaliland has claimed all overflights require a PPR from its own CAA, while Somalia has reaffirmed via AIC that it controls the entire HCSM/Mogadishu FIR; conflicting permit instructions should be expected near Hargeisa and northern Somalia.

cross.detail: The situation on the ground is highly unstable. The US prohibits flights in the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR below FL260, except for flights transiting the overwater portion going to/from HDAM/Djibouti. Several other countries have issued similar altitude-based warnings. Key events: Feb 2024: Multiple reports of aircraft in the Mogadishu FIR being contacted by a fake controller on the same frequency, issuing conflicting instructions. Aug 2023: Reports of uncontrolled combat helicopter operations at low levels (FL030) without position or routing information. Oct 2022: Somalian government warned that HCMM/Mogadishu airport may be targeted by militant groups. May 2022: Class A airspace implemented in the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR above FL245. 2020 - ongoing: Multiple Al-Shabaab attacks on HCMM/Mogadishu and nearby targets, including a UN compound. May 2020: An Embraer EMB-120 shot down on approach to Bardale airstrip, killing all six on board — an accidental shoot-down by Ethiopian forces combating Al-Shabaab.

OPKR.name: Baluchistan province (partial)
OPKR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPKR.narrative: Violent non-state actor (VNSA) groups with confirmed MANPADS operate in Baluchistan. The Kashmir dispute separately raises misidentification risk further north. The primary risks are from anti-aviation weaponry including MANPADS particularly below FL260, and inadvertent risk from military activity or misidentification in the Kashmir region. A ceasefire following four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in May 2025 has largely held, but the situation remains fragile.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in parts of western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions; current guidance generally advises remaining at or above FL260. Key events: Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; no new airspace closures issued and commercial traffic continues to transit OAKX/Kabul FIR including via P500 and G500. May 2025: Four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in the Kashmir region; ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held; some operators temporarily rerouted south via the Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024: Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan. Dec 2023 - ongoing: Crew reports of GPS spoofing in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in the Kashmir region, including airstrikes on both sides.

OPLR.name: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province (partial)
OPLR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPLR.narrative: Covers the north-western province, where the Kashmir dispute adds a misidentification risk on top of the VNSA activity common to both restricted Pakistani provinces. The primary risks are from anti-aviation weaponry including MANPADS particularly below FL260, and inadvertent risk from military activity or misidentification in the Kashmir region. GPS spoofing has been reported in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area from Dec 2023 onwards.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in parts of western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions; current guidance generally advises remaining at or above FL260. Key events: Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; no new airspace closures issued and commercial traffic continues to transit OAKX/Kabul FIR including via P500 and G500. May 2025: Four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in the Kashmir region; ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held; some operators temporarily rerouted south via the Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024: Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan. Dec 2023 - ongoing: Crew reports of GPS spoofing in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in the Kashmir region, including airstrikes on both sides.

OAKX.name: FIR Kabul
OAKX.conflictType: Post-conflict security vacuum — extremist groups active, limited air traffic services
OAKX.narrative: Since the 2021 Taliban takeover, Afghanistan has had little to no functioning air traffic control. The Kabul FIR is Class G airspace: crews use published contingency routes and TIBA procedures rather than normal ATC clearances. The primary risk is surface-to-air fire targeting aircraft at low altitudes; there is also an extreme threat to aircraft and crew on the ground. Traffic through the FIR increased in March 2026 as flights used the northern bypass route around the closed Middle East corridor. Some countries restrict overflights to airways P500 and G500 in the far east of the FIR; others allow overflights across the entire airspace at or above FL320.

cross.detail: The OAKX/Kabul FIR remains open but has no ATC service — it is uncontrolled Class G airspace following the withdrawal of US and allied forces in Aug 2021. Overflights must use specific contingency routes. Key events: March 2026: Traffic increased through the FIR as flights used the northern bypass route around the closed Middle East corridor. Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; commercial traffic continues to transit the FIR including via P500 and G500. Aug 2021: US and allied forces withdrew; the OAKX/Kabul FIR became uncontrolled Class G airspace with no ATC service.

HAAA.name: FIR Addis Ababa, north of 8.5°N
HAAA.conflictType: Regional/border tension — assessed by EASA as medium risk
HAAA.narrative: This is an EASA Information Note, not a CZIB — meaning EASA's risk assessment group judged the risk here as medium rather than high. Full analytical detail is restricted to the CZ Hub. The primary risk is large-scale ceasefire violations involving missiles or anti-aircraft weaponry, which could present a risk to overflying aircraft — either through misidentification or being caught in crossfire. A peace deal was agreed in Nov 2022 ending the conflict in the Tigray region, but airspace warnings from several states remain in place.
HAAA.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: The airspace risk picture in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region (the Ethiopia/Eritrea border) has improved since the Nov 2022 peace deal, but airspace warnings from several states remain in place. Key events: Feb 2024: New flare-up in fighting in the Amhara region (south of the Tigray region), including air strikes. Nov 2022: Peace deal agreed in the Tigray region; Ethiopian Airlines planned to resume flights to HAMK/Mekele airport. Nov 2021: Several western countries issued airspace and travel warnings for the Tigray region following increased fighting. July 2021: HAAA/Addis FIR published a NOTAM closing a section of airspace below FL290 over the Tigray region after reports that militia shot down a military transport plane near the capital Mekele. Nov 2020: Major escalation in the Tigray region; some airways closed by Ethiopian and Sudanese CAAs, including others close to the conflict zone frequently used on the Europe-East Africa route (UN321, UG300, UL432); multiple airports targeted by rockets; missiles fired into Eritrea targeting HHAS/Asmara; HABD/Bahir Dar and HAGN/Gondar also targeted. Sep 2018: Ethiopian ATC controllers went on strike; ATC service disrupted with unqualified replacement controllers brought in; strike ended Sep 7.

VYYF.name: FIR Yangon, below FL260
VYYF.conflictType: Internal armed conflict — assessed by EASA as medium risk
VYYF.narrative: As with Ethiopia, this is a medium-risk Information Note rather than a do-not-operate CZIB. France's own national guidance goes slightly further operationally, setting a hard altitude floor. The security situation has deteriorated since the military coup in Feb 2021, with conflict and violence across many parts of the country involving air strikes and armed clashes. GPS jamming and possible spoofing has also been reported in the north of the FIR for overflights between China and Bangladesh airspace.
VYYF.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: Several countries have issued airspace warnings at lower flight levels for the VYYF/Yangon FIR due to the potential risk from military operations, surface-to-air fire and anti-aviation weaponry. Key events: Jan 2024: Armed group shot down a military helicopter in the northern state of Kachin using a MANPAD. Sep 2023: Rebel group attacks on military targets across the country, including a makeshift drone dropping bombs on aircraft hangars at an airbase next to VYNT/Naypyitaw airport. Sep 2023: Reports of intermittent GPS jamming on airway N895 in the VYYF/Yangon FIR. Apr 2023: VYYY/Yangon temporarily closed following an attack by resistance groups using improvised artillery rounds. Sep 2022: A Myanmar National Airlines passenger reportedly shot as bullets passed through the fuselage of an ATR 72 on approach to VYLK/Loikaw. Feb 2021: Military coup ousted the government; ATC strike resulted in no ATC service for overflights, followed by increasing strikes, mass protests and armed clashes.
